title: Classic Synchronization Problems
summary: Producer-consumer, readers-writers, and dining philosophers — the standard worked case studies that show synchronization primitives applied to real coordination problems.

slides.markdown:
Three problems show up in essentially every OS course and interview loop: **producer-consumer**, **readers-writers**, and **dining philosophers**. They're not academic trivia — each one is a named, well-studied shape that a huge fraction of real concurrent systems reduce to, and knowing the standard solution (and its known failure modes) is genuinely load-bearing knowledge, not just a rite of passage.

This topic assumes you already know [semaphores](semaphores) and [monitors](monitors-and-condition-variables) — it's about applying those tools to three specific, well-known coordination shapes and knowing exactly where the naive solution to each one breaks.

slides.sectionTitle: Why these three problems are the standard interview vocabulary
slides.markdown:
Each of the three maps to a real, common system shape. **Producer-consumer** is any pipeline stage or queue — a web server's request queue, a logging pipeline, a task scheduler. **Readers-writers** is any data structure read far more often than it's updated — a config cache, a routing table, an in-memory index. **Dining philosophers** is the canonical shape for **deadlock from circular resource acquisition** — five threads each needing two of five shared resources is structurally identical to a database transaction that locks two rows in different orders.

Interviewers use them because they're compact enough to code in fifteen minutes but rich enough to expose whether you actually understand mutual exclusion, starvation, and deadlock, or just pattern-match "add a lock."

slides.sectionTitle: Producer-consumer / bounded buffer — full solution recap
slides.markdown:
One or more producer threads generate items into a fixed-size buffer; one or more consumer threads remove them. The constraints: producers must block when the buffer is full, consumers must block when it's empty, and the buffer's internal state must never be corrupted by concurrent access.

The standard solution — covered in full in the semaphores and monitors topics — uses either two counting semaphores (`empty`, `full`) plus a mutex, or a single mutex with two condition variables (`not_full`, `not_empty`). Both give the same guarantees; the monitor version is generally preferred in modern code for the reasons covered in that topic (encapsulation, harder to misuse).

The interview-relevant extension: with **multiple** producers or consumers (not just one of each), the mutex around the buffer access becomes load-bearing in a new way — two producers could otherwise race on the same insertion index — which is exactly why the mutex is separate from the counting semaphores in the classic solution.

Multiple threads share a data structure. **Readers** only inspect it and can safely run concurrently with each other. **Writers** modify it and need exclusive access — no reader or other writer may run at the same time as a writer. The goal is to allow as much read concurrency as possible while still guaranteeing writers see a consistent view and never race with anything.

This is a strictly harder problem than plain mutual exclusion: a solution that just uses one mutex for everything is *correct* but throws away all the concurrency benefit — readers serialize against each other for no reason, since concurrent reads can never corrupt anything. The interesting part of this problem is entirely about maximizing safe concurrency, not just achieving correctness.

slides.sectionTitle: First readers-writers solution and writer starvation
slides.markdown:
The classic first solution: a `read_count` variable (protected by its own small mutex) tracks how many readers are currently active. The first reader to arrive acquires the main resource lock (blocking out writers); the last reader to leave releases it. Readers in between just increment/decrement `read_count` and proceed freely. Writers simply acquire the main resource lock like normal, exclusive of everyone.

The bug: this solution gives **readers priority**. If readers keep arriving fast enough that `read_count` never drops to zero, a waiting writer never gets the main lock — it can wait indefinitely while a continuous stream of readers keeps the resource read-locked. This is **writer starvation**, and it's a completely realistic failure: a hot cache read by thousands of requests per second, with occasional writes, is exactly the shape where this bites in production.

slides.sectionTitle: Fixing writer starvation — the second readers-writers problem
slides.markdown:
The fix: once a writer is waiting, block any *new* readers from starting until that writer has gone. Concretely, add a check — before a reader proceeds, it first checks whether a writer is waiting (or holds the lock) and if so, waits itself, even though no writer currently holds the resource. This gives writers priority over any reader that arrives after them, guaranteeing a waiting writer eventually gets in once the currently-active readers finish.

This "writers-preference" variant fixes writer starvation but can itself starve readers if writers arrive back-to-back continuously — there's no free lunch. Production reader-writer lock implementations (like Java's `ReentrantReadWriteLock` in fair mode, or pthreads' `PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NP`) typically pick an explicit policy and document it, precisely because "readers-writers" isn't one problem with one right answer — it's a family with a tunable fairness trade-off.

slides.sectionTitle: Dining philosophers: the setup and the deadlock risk
slides.markdown:
Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks between them (one fork shared between each adjacent pair). Each philosopher alternates thinking and eating; to eat, a philosopher needs **both** forks adjacent to them — left and right. The naive solution: each philosopher picks up their left fork, then their right fork.

The deadlock: if all five philosophers pick up their left fork at exactly the same moment, every fork is now held, and every philosopher is stuck waiting forever for their right fork, which is somebody else's left fork. This is **circular wait** made concrete — the same structural bug behind real deadlocks like two database transactions each locking rows in opposite order.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: dining philosophers table with forks
slides.markdown:
![Dining philosophers deadlock scenario](assets/dining-philosophers.svg)

The diagram's key detail: there are exactly as many forks as philosophers, which is what makes the naive left-then-right strategy able to deadlock everyone simultaneously — if there were one spare fork, at least one philosopher could always eat.

slides.sectionTitle: Breaking the symmetry: resource ordering, arbitrator, odd/even solutions
slides.markdown:
All standard fixes work by breaking the symmetry that let all five philosophers deadlock in lockstep. **Resource ordering**: number the forks, and require every philosopher to pick up the lower-numbered fork first — this guarantees at least one philosopher (the one whose "left" happens to be the higher-numbered fork) picks up the globally-lower fork second, breaking the circular wait. **Arbitrator (waiter)**: add a single mutex a philosopher must acquire before picking up either fork, limiting how many philosophers can even attempt to eat concurrently to four — guaranteeing at least one succeeds. **Odd/even**: odd-numbered philosophers pick up their left fork first, even-numbered pick up their right fork first — same effect as resource ordering, framed differently.

All three share the same underlying principle, which is the actual interview-relevant idea: **deadlock requires circular wait, so any fix that provably breaks the cycle (via ordering, or via limiting concurrent attempts) is sufficient** — you don't need to add more forks or eliminate mutual exclusion.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: what each classic problem teaches
slides.markdown:
| Problem | Core hazard it teaches | Real-world shape |
|---|---|---|
| Producer-consumer | Coordinating a bounded shared buffer between roles with different responsibilities | Queues, pipelines, message brokers |
| Readers-writers | Maximizing safe concurrency, not just achieving correctness; fairness trade-offs | Caches, config stores, in-memory indexes |
| Dining philosophers | Circular wait as the root cause of deadlock, and how to structurally prevent it | Multi-lock acquisition, distributed transactions, database row locking |

A useful interview framing: producer-consumer and readers-writers are both fundamentally about *throughput under correctness constraints*, while dining philosophers is fundamentally about *avoiding a specific failure mode (deadlock)* — naming which axis a real system's bug sits on is what separates "I've seen this pattern" from "I memorized three names."

slides.sectionTitle: Recognizing dining philosophers in a real codebase
slides.markdown:
The dining philosophers shape appears in production far more often than the toy version suggests, usually disguised as "acquire multiple locks." The most common real instance: two database transactions, T1 locking row A then row B, and T2 locking row B then row A concurrently — structurally identical to two adjacent philosophers each grabbing their left fork first. Most production databases actually detect this automatically (a **deadlock detector** watching the wait-for graph) and abort one transaction to break the cycle, which is why you sometimes see a "deadlock detected, transaction rolled back" error under concurrent load rather than a true hang.

Application-level code rarely gets this safety net — acquiring two mutexes in inconsistent order across two code paths is a classic, hard-to-reproduce deadlock that shows up only under specific timing, exactly like dining philosophers. The staff-level habit: whenever code needs to hold more than one lock at a time, establish and document a global lock ordering (e.g., "always lock by ascending object ID") across the whole codebase, not just within one function — a locally-consistent order in one file doesn't help if another file acquires the same two locks in the opposite order.
